name: bridge-coding-v1
description: R2-BRIDGE-01 fresh held-out coding specification. New task (longest increasing subsequence, O(n log n)), authored for this bridge holdout only; not a reuse or paraphrase of any Research2 DEV or EVAL coding prompt.

items.prompt: Write a Python function `longest_increasing_subsequence(nums)` that returns the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of a list of integers, using an O(n log n) algorithm (patience sorting with binary search), not the naive O(n^2) dynamic program. Include a short docstring explaining the approach, and 4 example assertions covering: a strictly increasing input, a strictly decreasing input, an input with duplicate values, and an empty list. Then briefly explain why the binary-search step preserves correctness even though the auxiliary array it maintains is not itself the actual subsequence.

cli_split_field_note: argine.research.cli's 'research trace --split' flag only accepts {dev, eval} (argine/research/cli.py 'trace' subparser, choices=['dev','eval']); there is no third CLI-level split value. Per the loader (argine/research/workloads.py:load, the 'items'-schema fallback branch), the CLI-facing 'split' field here is literal plumbing selecting which dict key the prompts load under -- it is set to the already-supported value 'eval' so this file can be captured with the existing CLI and loader, with NO code change. The true provenance-level identity of this corpus (a fresh BRIDGE holdout, distinct from and never to be confused with the R2-09 EVAL corpus) is tracked entirely by workload_id, file path, output directory, and the 'provenance_split_identity' field above plus experiments/R2-BRIDGE-01-retention-feasibility/dev_holdout_separation.json -- exactly mirroring how R2-09's own EVAL corpus is externally distinguished from R2-08's DEV corpus by workload_id/path/manifest, not by a unique CLI split string.
